issues.subcategory: simulated data presented as empirical results
issues.description: The entire Method and Results sections are based on randomly generated Qualtrics data, not data collected from real participants. The manuscript repeatedly acknowledges this with bracketed warnings but still presents statistical outputs, effect sizes, significance tests, and interpretations as if they represent genuine empirical findings. Submitting or evaluating a manuscript with fabricated results—even disclosed simulations—means no validity claim can be assessed. No conclusion about replication success or failure is possible.
issues.quote: [IMPORTANT: Method and results sections were written using randomized dataset produced by Qualtrics to simulate what these sections will look like after data collection. These will be updated following the data collection.]

issues.subcategory: self-selection into experimental conditions eliminates random assignment
issues.description: The procedures state that 'Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions.' Random assignment is the foundational requirement for causal inference in experimental research. Allowing participants to self-select into intervention versus no-intervention, and identifiable versus statistical versus joint conditions, introduces massive self-selection confounds (e.g., participants more motivated to help may select identifiable victim conditions; analytically-minded participants may select the intervention condition). This design cannot support any causal claim about the effect of intervention or identifiability on donation or feelings.
issues.quote: Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions.

issues.subcategory: within-subject design label misapplied to what is a between-subjects design
issues.description: The design section explicitly states 'We embedded Studies 1 and 3 of Small et al. (2007) into a single within-subject design with identifiability and intervention as the independent variables.' However, the entire structure of the study—separate conditions for identifiable, statistical, and joint victims, and separate intervention/no-intervention groups—is a between-subjects design. Each participant is assigned to one cell of the 2×3 design. The original studies by Small et al. were also between-subjects. Labeling this as within-subject is a fundamental design description error that affects power calculations, appropriate statistical models, and interpretation of results.
issues.quote: We embedded Studies 1 and 3 of Small et al. (2007) into a single within-subject design with identifiability and intervention as the independent variables

issues.subcategory: group means reversed in results text relative to descriptive statistics table
issues.description: The results text reports: 'participants who faced a statistical victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the identifiable victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67).' However, computing marginal means from Table 7 yields the opposite: Identifiable condition mean ≈ (2.58×159 + 2.50×175)/334 ≈ 2.54, and Statistical condition mean ≈ (2.46×175 + 2.01×159)/334 ≈ 2.25. The text has inverted which condition has the higher mean. This means the narrative interpretation of who donates more is factually incorrect relative to the manuscript's own descriptive table.
issues.quote: participants who faced a statistical victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the identifiable victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67)

issues.subcategory: abstract finding on perceived impact contradicts stated hypothesis and actual results
issues.description: Three separate inconsistencies converge on the perceived impact measure. (1) Hypothesis 6 states: 'An identifiable victim elicits higher perceived impact of donation than statistical victims' (identifiable > statistical). (2) The abstract claims: 'Results have supported the hypothesis that people have a lower rating of perceived impact of donation when they faced an identifiable victim'—which is the opposite direction from Hypothesis 6. (3) The actual significant result in Table 14 is that statistical victims have higher perceived impact than the joint condition (Statistical VS Joint: p=.041), while neither Identifiable VS Statistical (p=1.000) nor Identifiable VS Joint (p=.359) are significant. The abstract mischaracterizes both the hypothesis and the actual significant finding.
issues.quote: Results have supported the hypothesis that people have a lower rating of perceived impact of donation when they faced an identifiable victim or an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics.

issues.subcategory: no correction for multiple comparisons across 18 tests for segregated feelings
issues.description: Table 13 reports 18 separate statistical tests (6 feeling variables × 3 effects: identifiability, intervention, interaction). No correction for multiple comparisons is applied or even mentioned. With alpha=.05 and 18 tests, approximately 0.9 false positives are expected by chance alone. The only significant result—identifiability on perceived impact (p=.045)—would not survive even a conservative Bonferroni correction (adjusted alpha = .05/18 = .0028). The extension's main finding rests entirely on this uncorrected test.
issues.quote: only the result of identifiability on the perceived impact of donation yielded significant findings... F... p... .045*

issues.subcategory: incorrect df2 in Table 1 for original study
issues.description: Table 1 reports all effects from the original Study 1 with df2=115 (N=121, 2×2 ANOVA). In a 2×2 between-subjects ANOVA with N=121, the residual degrees of freedom should be N − k = 121 − 4 = 117, not 115. This is confirmed within the manuscript itself: Table 11 reports the original study contrast test with df=117. The inconsistent df values across tables suggest either an error in the ANOVA df or in the contrast test df, and the reported F-statistics and p-values may be based on incorrect degrees of freedom.
issues.quote: Identifiability ... df1=1, df2=115 ... Intervention ... df1=1, df2=115 ... Interaction ... df1=1, df2=115

issues.subcategory: same F-statistic and parameters reported for both factor levels and the overall effect in Table 1
issues.description: Table 1 reports the F-statistic, df, p-value, and ηp² for 'Identifiability' as a factor, then repeats the exact same values (F=6.75, df1=1, df2=115, p<.05, ηp²=.06) for the sub-rows 'Identifiable victim' (M=2.12) and 'Statistical victim' (M=1.21) as if these are separate tests. These sub-rows represent condition means (levels of the factor), not separate statistical tests. Listing test statistics for the levels of a factor as if they were independent tests is a reporting error that misrepresents the structure of the ANOVA.

issues.subcategory: biologically impossible demographic values in simulated sample
issues.description: The simulated participant sample reports Mage=67.80, SD=30.10, with an age range of 18–120. An age of 120 is biologically implausible; this is the maximum randomly generated value from Qualtrics. The mean age of 67.80 is also implausible for an Amazon Mechanical Turk sample, which typically skews toward 25–45 years old. An SD of 30.10 is anomalously large. These values confirm the randomized nature of the dataset but are reported without critical commentary, undermining any claim that the simulated sample resembles the target population.
issues.quote: A total of 1000 responses were generated from the Qualtrics for pre-registration (Mage = 67.80, SD=30.10; 471 females and 529 males)... Age range (years) | 18-120

issues.subcategory: Bonferroni-adjusted p-value is significant while 95% CI for d includes zero
issues.description: Table 10 reports that the Identifiable VS Statistical comparison yields pBonferroni=.049 (statistically significant at alpha=.05 after Bonferroni correction for 3 comparisons, implying p_raw ≈ .016), yet the reported 95% CI for Cohen's d is [-0.05, 0.20], which includes zero. If the raw p ≈ .016, the standard 95% CI for d should exclude zero. This internal contradiction suggests either the CI was not calculated to correspond to the significance test, the p-value calculation is incorrect, or the Bonferroni correction was misapplied. The result cannot be both significant at a Bonferroni-adjusted alpha and have a 95% CI spanning zero.

issues.subcategory: no manipulation check for the deliberative thinking intervention
issues.description: The core experimental manipulation—teaching participants about the identifiable victim effect to induce deliberative thinking—has no associated manipulation check. There is no measure verifying that participants read, understood, or were influenced by the intervention materials. Without a manipulation check, a null result for the intervention effect cannot be distinguished from intervention failure (participants ignored or did not process the materials) versus a genuine absence of the debiasing effect. This is especially important since the study's key hypothesis (H2, H3) concerns the intervention's effectiveness.
issues.quote: Learning about the identifiable victim effect reduces people's donation tendency... Explicitly learning about the identifiable victim effect reduces donation to an identifiable victim but not to statistical victims

issues.subcategory: imaginary donation replaces real monetary donation—fundamentally different construct
issues.description: The original study used real money ($5 received by participants beforehand) donated to an actual charity (Save the Children) via a signed request letter. The replication substitutes an imaginary donation ('indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5'). Hypothetical and real donations are known to differ substantially in magnitude and sensitivity to experimental manipulations (hypothetical donation bias). This DV change is classified as 'Different' in Table 6 but downplayed as a minor deviation. This is particularly critical because the identifiable victim effect's theoretical significance lies in its real-world consequences for charitable behavior.
issues.quote: Imaginary donation: Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5 to the corresponding victim(s) instead of donating the money to Save the Children after signing a charity request letter.

issues.subcategory: causal language applied to quasi-experimental self-selected conditions
issues.description: Throughout the manuscript, causal language is used ('reduces giving,' 'intervention effect,' 'explicit learning reduces donation,' 'thinking analytically reduces motivation') even though participants self-selected into conditions rather than being randomly assigned. Without random assignment, observed differences between conditions cannot be attributed causally to the manipulation. Confounders such as motivation to help, prior charitable behavior, cognitive style, and political orientation may systematically vary between self-selected groups and drive any observed differences.
issues.quote: Explicitly learning about the identifiable victim effect reduces donation to an identifiable victim but not to statistical victims... thinking analytically about your helping behaviour would reduce your motivation to offer assistance

issues.subcategory: analysis conducted and reported on simulated data before real data collection, enabling post-hoc analytic decisions
issues.description: The analysis pipeline was fully executed and reported on a random dataset before actual data collection. While the intent is to pre-specify analyses, presenting complete results tables, post-hoc tests, specific test statistics (t, F, p, d, CIs), and narrative interpretations creates opportunities for analytic flexibility: the analysis code and choices may be adjusted after seeing simulated outputs to optimize the pipeline, then applied to real data in ways that are not fully pre-registered. The pre-registration link is provided but deviations between the pre-registration and the reported analysis plan are not explicitly audited in the main text.
issues.quote: Results were written using randomized dataset produced by Qualtrics to simulate what these sections will look like after data collection. These will be updated following the data collection.

issues.subcategory: availability heuristic misapplied to explain emotional responses to identifiable victims
issues.description: The manuscript invokes the 'availability heuristic' (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973) to explain why identifiable victims elicit greater emotional responses, stating it is 'activated when we value a personalized individual.' The availability heuristic concerns the ease of retrieving instances from memory to estimate frequency or probability—it is not a mechanism for generating sympathy or affect. The appropriate frameworks here are the affect heuristic (Slovic et al., 2007, cited elsewhere in the manuscript), narrative transportation, or imagery-based processing. This is a theoretical misattribution that weakens the conceptual framing.
issues.quote: The 'availability heuristic' (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973), which relies on the ease of retrieving relevant instances from memory, is believed to be activated when we value a personalized individual (Small & Loewenstein, 2003). The information we receive about this person may elicit stronger affective reactions such as sympathy and distress

issues.subcategory: merging two separate studies into one experiment without adequately addressing confounds introduced
issues.description: Studies 1 and 3 of Small et al. (2007) were designed as separate experiments with different participant pools and designs (2×2 vs. one-way). Merging them adds the joint condition to Study 1's 2×2 design and adds intervention to Study 3's three-condition design, creating a 2×3 factorial design that was never tested in the original work. This introduces new cell combinations (e.g., joint+intervention) that have no original counterpart, making direct comparison to original findings ambiguous. The authors acknowledge this but understate its implications for replication interpretation.
issues.quote: we merged Studies 1 and 3 into one single experiment to study both the explicit and implicit intervention of debiasing the identifiable victim effect... The intervention of learning about the effect would also be applied to the joint condition to reveal a more comprehensive comparison

issues.subcategory: exclusion criteria applied but post-exclusion sample size not reported
issues.description: The methods state that participants with prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect and those failing attention checks were excluded, but no information is provided on how many participants were excluded on each criterion or what the final analytic sample size was. The 1000 figure appears to be the pre-exclusion simulated total. This omission prevents evaluation of attrition patterns, potential selection effects from exclusions, and whether sufficient power remained after exclusions.
issues.quote: Participants who indicated they had prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect were excluded, as well as those who failed the attention check.

issues.subcategory: no ethics approval, IRB statement, or informed consent disclosure
issues.description: The manuscript contains no statement regarding ethics committee or IRB approval, and no description of how informed consent was obtained from participants. This is a standard reporting requirement for human subjects research in psychology and is required by APA ethical principles and most journals. Its complete absence is a significant reporting gap.
issues.quote: Declaration of Conflict of Interest: The author(s) declared no potential conflicts of interest... Financial Disclosure/Funding: The author(s) received no financial support

issues.subcategory: replication classified as 'close to very close' despite multiple operationally significant deviations
issues.description: The replication is classified as 'close to very close' but involves multiple substantial deviations: (1) real money replaced by hypothetical donation (critical DV difference); (2) laboratory replaced by online MTurk (setting and population change); (3) two separate studies merged into one factorial design; (4) updated victim stimuli; (5) feelings measured in the joint condition (not done originally); (6) self-selection rather than random assignment. The DV operationalization row in Table 6 is classified as 'Similar' and Physical settings as 'Different,' yet the combination of these changes makes the study closer to a conceptual replication. Overstating proximity to the original limits appropriate interpretation of non-replication.
issues.quote: Replication classification | close to very close replication

issues.subcategory: ordered probit regression dropped without adequate statistical justification
issues.description: The original study analyzed the discrete donation variable (0–5 dollars in integer increments) using ordered probit regression, which is statistically appropriate for ordinal bounded outcomes. The replication explicitly states 'This test would not be conducted in the replication' and substitutes ANOVA. Using ANOVA on an ordinal 6-point scale (0–5) violates the assumption of continuous normally distributed outcomes. No statistical rationale is provided for this deviation, and it may produce different results from ordinal models, particularly given the bounded nature of the scale.
issues.quote: Ordered probit regression... effect of identifiability on donation... This test would not be conducted in the replication

issues.subcategory: key document links are placeholder text, rendering pre-registration and materials inaccessible
issues.description: Two of the four critical project links in the Important Links table contain literal placeholder text rather than actual URLs. Additionally, the supplementary document (which is referenced repeatedly for power analysis, design tables, procedure details, and deviation reporting) is linked externally and cannot be evaluated as part of the submission. Multiple cross-references to supplementary sections (e.g., 'Power analysis of the original study effect,' 'Comparisons and deviations,' 'Table of design') cannot be verified.
issues.quote:
Cloud folder for presentation (PPT and PDF) | <enter link here>
Cloud folder for peer reviews | <enter link here>

issues.subcategory: interaction effect significant without significant main effect—direction of interaction unspecified
issues.description: Table 9 reports a significant interaction of identifiability × intervention (F(2,994)=4.25, p=.015) in the absence of a significant main effect of intervention (F(1,994)=0.50, p=.480). While this is statistically possible, the manuscript provides no plot of the interaction pattern and no post-hoc decomposition of the significant interaction. The nature of the interaction is therefore uninterpretable. Claiming results are 'contrary to the original' for the intervention main effect while having a significant interaction requires clarification of what the interaction means theoretically.
issues.quote: Replication | 2 | 4.25 | .015* | .008 ... Intervention ... Replication | 1 | 0.50 | .480 | .001

issues.subcategory: cell sizes in tables do not reflect exclusion of ineligible participants
issues.description: Tables 7 and 8 show cell sizes summing to exactly 1000 (e.g., 159+175+166+175+159+166=1000), which is the total number of Qualtrics-generated responses before any exclusions. Since the methods describe excluding participants with prior knowledge and those failing attention checks, the post-exclusion sample should be smaller. The reported analyses appear to use the full simulated dataset without applying the stated exclusion criteria, making the sample description inconsistent with the analysis.
issues.quote: A total of 1000 responses were generated from the Qualtrics for pre-registration... Participants who indicated they had prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect were excluded, as well as those who failed the attention check.

issues.subcategory: significant perceived impact finding is in direction opposite to the stated hypothesis
issues.description: Hypothesis 6 predicts 'An identifiable victim elicits higher perceived impact of donation than statistical victims' (identifiable > statistical). The only significant post-hoc finding for perceived impact is Statistical VS Joint (t(994)=2.47, p=.041), indicating that statistical victims yield higher perceived impact than the joint condition—the opposite direction. The Identifiable VS Statistical comparison is p=1.000. The authors present this as supporting Hypothesis 6 in the abstract, but neither the significant comparison nor its direction corresponds to the pre-specified hypothesis. This constitutes both a conceptual error and an overclaim of support.
issues.quote: Significant differences were found between the statistical victim condition and the joint condition... participants who faced a statistical victim (M=3.12, SD=1.43) had a higher rating of perceived impact... An identifiable victim elicits higher perceived impact of donation than statistical victims

issues.subcategory: standard deviations missing for all Study 3 conditions in Table 2
issues.description: Table 2 summarizing Study 3 results from the original article reports N/A for all standard deviations, preventing calculation of effect sizes, confidence intervals, or adequate power analysis for the Study 3 component of the replication. While attributed to non-reporting in the original, this gap means the power analysis for Study 3 (d=0.23, 95%CI [0.01, 0.45]) relies on incomplete information, and its accuracy cannot be verified.
issues.quote: Identifiable victim | 2.38 | N/A ... Statistical victim | 1.14 | N/A ... Identifiable victim with statistics | 1.43 | N/A

issues.subcategory: Hypothesis 5a references 'identifiable victim' in the comparison description but should reference all three conditions
issues.description: Hypothesis 5a states 'An identifiable victim elicits more affective feelings than an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics and statistical victims.' This hypothesis compares identifiable to both other conditions but is listed as a single hypothesis. The original Study 1 had only two identifiability conditions (identifiable and statistical), so this formulation extending to a three-way comparison was not tested in the original. Furthermore, Hypothesis 5b predicts that intervention reduces feelings toward identifiable and joint but not statistical victims, which introduces asymmetric predictions not clearly mapped to the merged design.
issues.quote:
5a: An identifiable victim elicits more affective feelings than an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics and statistical victims
5b: Learning about the identifiable victim effect elicits less affective feelings towards an identifiable victim and identifiable victims with victim statistics but not towards statistical victims

issues.subcategory: population shift from US university students to MTurk workers not adequately discussed as moderator
issues.description: The original study recruited participants at a student center of a university in Pennsylvania (US students), while the replication uses Amazon Mechanical Turk workers. MTurk workers differ from university students in age, education, socioeconomic status, prior charitable giving experience, and motivation for task completion. These differences may moderate the identifiable victim effect. The manuscript briefly mentions this as a contextual variable difference but does not discuss how these population differences could affect the magnitude or direction of the target effect, which is important for interpreting replication failure.
issues.quote: MTurk workers as participants: We will recruit participants on the Mechanical Amazon Turk platform while the original study recruited participants sitting inside the school centre of a university in Pennsylvania
